name: clean-architecture
context: Software systems requiring strong separation between business logic and external frameworks, databases, and UI layers. Clean Architecture, defined by Robert C. Martin, organizes a system into concentric layers with a strict dependency rule: dependencies point inward only. The outermost layer (Frameworks & Drivers) contains details like databases and web frameworks; the innermost layer (Entities) contains enterprise business rules that are framework-agnostic and maximally reusable. This pattern is for teams building long-lived, maintainable applications where the domain logic must remain testable, portable, and independent of infrastructure choices. It complements hexagonal architecture's ports-and-adapters concept but adds explicit layer naming and the dependency rule as a first-class constraint.
benefits: Framework independence: business logic never imports from UI, database, or web framework packages
Testability: enterprise rules can be tested with nothing more than in-memory data structures
Independence of delivery mechanism: the same business logic runs as a CLI tool, a REST API, or a background job
Database independence: business logic has no knowledge of how data is persisted; repositories are an interface, not an implementation
Clear dependency structure: new developers immediately understand what can import what
Portable business rules: entities and use cases can be reused across multiple applications
Reduced technical debt: explicit interfaces prevent framework coupling from accumulating silently
tradeoffs: Initial boilerplate: establishing the layer structure and dependency rules requires upfront investment
Indirection overhead: every business operation passes through multiple abstraction layers
Learning curve: developers accustomed to framework-centric layouts need time to understand the inward-dependency rule
Ceremony for simple operations: CRUD operations that are trivial in Rails/Django require more structure
Interface proliferation: each use case typically defines its own input/output models, leading to many small classes
Dual persistence concerns: reconciling clean architecture's preference for domain purity with ORM expectations can be complex
Over-engineering risk for small projects: the layer count and interface discipline is heavyweight for simple applications
use_cases: A financial trading platform where the order validation rules must work identically whether the input comes from a web UI, a mobile app, or an API
A healthcare system where patient record logic must remain portable across different database technologies as regulatory requirements evolve
An e-commerce platform where domain logic is tested in isolation without needing a running database or web server
A SaaS multi-tenant application where tenant-specific customizations must not pollute the core domain model
avoid_when: The application is simple CRUD where a framework's defaults already provide adequate structure
The team is new to layered architecture and the learning curve would delay delivery
Strict latency requirements make the additional indirection of multiple layers unacceptable
The project is a prototype that will be discarded after validation
The organization has standardized on a framework-centric architecture and would resist the cleaner-dependency approach
component_types: Entities: Enterprise business rules that are framework-agnostic and contain the core of the domain model
Use Cases (Interactors): Application-specific business rules that orchestrate entities to accomplish a user goal
Interface Adapters: Converters that translate between data formats convenient for use cases/entities and those convenient for external agents
Controllers and Presenters: Interface adapter implementations that handle user input and presentation logic
Repository Interfaces: Port definitions in the use case layer that data access must fulfill, decoupling from any specific ORM
External Interfaces: Database implementations, web framework glue code, UI components — the outermost layer that depends inward
DTOs (Data Transfer Objects): Simple data structures crossing layer boundaries, holding no business logic
anti_patterns: The Lonely Use Case: use cases that are thin wrappers around repository calls, providing no real business logic but adding indirection
Anemic Entities: entities that are pure data classes with no behavior, defeating the purpose of having business rules at the innermost layer
Framework-in-the-Core: importing Django models or Spring components into the domain layer, breaking the dependency rule
God Objects at the Use Case Layer: use cases that know too much and orchestrate too many entities, becoming a maintenance bottleneck
Repository Implementations Leaking Upward: concrete database types appearing in use case signatures instead of interface abstractions
Skipped Layers: collapsing the interface adapter layer, causing framework code to appear directly in use cases
design_principles: Dependency Rule: source code dependencies must point only inward, toward higher-level policies; no inner-layer module may mention anything from an outer layer
Entities First: start by modeling the domain's business rules as plain objects with no framework dependencies
Use Cases as Application Scripts: each use case is a single-responsibility class with one public method, orchestrating entities and repositories
Repository Ports, Not Implementations: data access is always an interface in the use case layer; the implementation is injected from the outer layer
Frameworks Are Plugins: treat web frameworks, ORMs, and UI components as external plugins; keep their imports at the outer layer boundary
Test the Inner Layers First: entities and use cases are tested without any external infrastructure; database and UI tests come last
One Data Structure Per Layer Boundary: DTOs crossing layer boundaries are simple, structure-only objects; no behavior, no framework types
best_practices: Enforce the Dependency Rule with Static Analysis: use tools like SonarQube or ArchUnit to fail builds when inward dependencies are violated
Name Layers by What They Contain: Entities (domain model), Use Cases (application logic), Adapters (interface converters), Frameworks (infrastructure)
Keep Entities Rich: business rule methods belong in entities; do not strip entities to pure getters/setters
Separate Input and Output Models: use case input and output are different classes; this prevents caller changes from propagating inward
Repository Interfaces Live Close to Use Cases: define the port where it is used, not in a separate infrastructure package
Rotate Frameworks Without Touching Domain: verify that swapping from Django to FastAPI requires changes only in the outermost layer
Structure Tests by Layer: entity tests are fastest and have no mocks; use case tests use in-memory repositories; adapter tests are integration tests
